title: You Must Put On A Dance
author: Michael Perrone
summary: Michael Perrone argues that modern school and church dances fail because young people are gathered to play a game no one has taught them. He describes traditional dancing as a cooperative social technology in which men and women play complementary roles, with rules that absorb the awkwardness of approaching one another and turn acquaintances into friends and romances. Perrone places the blame not on kids but on adults stuck in 'restriction mode', so focused on keeping a dangerous game safe that they forgot to teach it, leaving teens to invent social conventions on their own. His remedy is simple: put on a genuine dance, as his family did with a church gym, borrowed speakers, and the Virginia Reel. The second half interviews Nelson, who organizes an annual family ball in Texas aimed at building community, patronage among friends, and, over the long term, healthy on-ramps to courtship and family formation outside mainstream dating culture.
points: Perrone reframes dancing as a cooperative game with rules that give young men and women a socially legible way to interact.
Modern dances are mediated spaces where fear of being recorded and the absence of shared forms leave the dance floor a no-man's land.
Adults, not kids, caused the decline by restricting the game without teaching it.
His family's dance showed teens that the Virginia Reel was fun and made talking to a partner easier.
The Texas ball Nelson describes aims to create a vetted community courting pool while patronizing friends' businesses.
quotes: Dancing is an unmediated space for men and women to relate. All the ambiguity and awkwardness of talking to a girl brushed aside, absorbed by the rules of the game.
Dancing is an amazing social technology; turning strangers and acquaintances into friends and romantic interest into relationships.
It’s caused by adults stuck in restriction mode; so concerned with making sure the dangerous game isn’t too dangerous that we forgot to teach the game.
We’ve built an environment in which young people are expected to spontaneously produce their own social conventions. (No wonder everyone is so anxious.)

The teenagers were totally shocked to learn that dancing the Virginia Reel is a lot of fun. And one teenage boy was stunned about how much easier it was to cut through the awkwardness and talk to his dancing partner.
The biggest, most audacious goal of a ball is ultimately giving our kids on-ramps to courting and family formation outside of the really corrosive mainstream dating paradigm.

Your kids are going to be like your spouse, and your grandkids are going to be like your tribe, the group of people who are around. So, can we build a group of people that we wouldn’t mind our grandkids being like?
